passage: Monday. Devika refused the green bottle at water time. "Kiran and Mihir and Tara have blue ones," she said, clutching her blue lid. Tara shrugged and went on drinking. Thursday. The four of them played shop. Devika said the rule was that everyone must be the shopkeeper, and Mihir agreed at once; Kiran frowned but said nothing. Next Tuesday. The teacher gave out red and yellow ribbons for the dance. Devika looked at Kiran's, took the same colour, and danced the same step a beat behind him, smiling only when he smiled back.

qa.q: Why did Devika clutch the blue lid on Monday?
qa.a: Devika clutched the blue lid because Kiran, Mihir and Tara have blue ones.

qa.q: What might Devika feel when her ribbon matches Kiran's and Kiran smiles back?
qa.a: Devika seems to feel safe and included; smiling only when Kiran smiles suggests sameness reassures Devika.

qa.q: What small step could the teacher take to help Devika feel safe while trying something different?
qa.a: The teacher could let Devika keep one thing the same as the group and try one small difference beside another child, so being different is not lonely.

qa.q: How might Kiran feel about Devika's shop rule that everyone must be the shopkeeper?
qa.a: Kiran frowns but says nothing, which suggests Kiran is unhappy with the rule but would rather keep the game going than argue.

grounding: A child wants the same bottle, game rule and dance step as the group because sameness feels safe, shown across three days.

passage: Rain drummed on the roof, so the sports-day dance was squeezed into the tiny library with ten minutes left before the buses. The teacher showed a new step: two claps and a jump. Kunal did it at once, then Ravi and Sana. Yogesh stood still, watching their feet. "Everybody is doing the same one," he whispered, and copied them, one beat late. Only Hema kept her old arm wave. Yogesh glanced at her, edged closer to Kunal, and did not look at Hema again until the bell rang.

qa.q: Why was the sports-day dance practised in the tiny library?
qa.a: Rain drummed on the roof, so the sports-day dance was squeezed into the tiny library.

qa.q: Why did Yogesh copy the new step one beat late?
qa.a: Yogesh saw everybody doing the same step and whispered that they were all doing the same one, so copying felt safer than standing out; the feeling is a wish to belong.

qa.q: What could the teacher say to Yogesh that keeps both belonging and difference possible?
qa.a: The teacher could say that a group can share one dance and still let a person add a small touch, so being different is not the same as being left out.

qa.q: What might it be like for Hema to keep her arm wave while the others do the new step?
qa.a: Hema may feel a little alone yet sure of her own step; Hema keeps going even when Yogesh glances over and edges away.

grounding: A child insists on the same dance step as the group, and time pressure in a cramped room makes sameness feel safer than difference.

passage:
“Not green,” Rajni said, pushing the bottle back across the shop counter. “Purple.”
Papa sighed. The Karol Bagh shop was crowded. “Green is nice. It has a frog on it.”
“Tina has purple. Gudiya has purple. Mehr has purple.” Her chin wobbled. “If I have green, I'm not in the purple group.”
Her brother Hemant rolled his eyes. “There's no purple group.”
“There is!” Rajni's voice cracked. “We sit together.”
The shopkeeper searched a shelf and found one purple bottle, slightly scratched. Rajni hugged it as if it were a puppy. Papa paid, smiling a little.

qa.q: How many friends did Rajni name who have purple bottles?
qa.a: She named three: Tina, Gudiya and Mehr.

qa.q: Why did Rajni's chin wobble at the counter?
qa.a: She felt worried and left out; a green bottle would mean she was not part of the purple group her friends sit in.

qa.q: How could Papa respond to Rajni's worry if there had been no purple bottle?
qa.a: He could take her feeling seriously, say she is still Tina's and Mehr's friend whatever colour she carries, and let her pick a sticker to share with them.

qa.q: How does Hemant see the fuss?
qa.a: To Hemant it looks silly; he says there's no purple group because he doesn't see how much sameness means to his sister.

grounding: Shows a young child insisting on the same bottle colour as her friends because being different feels like being left out.

passage:
“No, Payal, it's hand up, then turn!” Bhavna said, spinning in the living room.
“I did turn!” Payal stamped. “I want to do it like you and Gauri.”
Gauri showed her again. “Hand up, turn, clap.”
Payal tried. Her clap came first. Bhavna giggled. Payal's face crumpled. “Now I'm doing a different dance. I'm not in it.”
Bhavna's mother put down the cake knife. “Payal, you can stand in the middle. Watch Gauri's hands and I'll count.”
“One, two, three!” All three girls turned together. Payal clapped exactly with them and grinned so wide she forgot to bow.

qa.q: Which steps did Gauri show Payal?
qa.a: Gauri showed her: hand up, turn, clap.

qa.q: What was Payal feeling when her clap came first?
qa.a: She felt hurt and shut out; she said she was doing a different dance and was not in it.

qa.q: What small step helped Payal join in?
qa.a: Bhavna's mother put her in the middle to watch Gauri's hands and counted aloud, so she could move at the same time as the others.

qa.q: What might Bhavna's giggle have felt like from Payal's side?
qa.a: It probably stung, because to Payal a mistake meant being outside the group, not just a funny moment.

grounding: Shows a child who wants to do the same dance step as her friends and feels left out when she is different.

passage:
Kindergarten note, Class UKG-B, Monday.
In outdoor time, Farhan refused to play tag with the rule the children at his table had chosen. He kept saying, “Madhuri's group says you're safe on the swings. We have to play that way.” When two boys said the slide was safe too, Farhan sat on the sand and cried. I asked him what felt bad. He said, “Then we are not the same as them.” I invited Madhuri's group over, and the children agreed on one rule together. Farhan ran off smiling. I'll share this with his parents at pickup.

qa.q: What did Madhuri's group say about the swings?
qa.a: Madhuri's group said you're safe on the swings.

qa.q: Why did Farhan sit on the sand and cry?
qa.a: He felt upset and anxious because a different rule meant his table would not be the same as Madhuri's group.

qa.q: How did the teacher help, and what else could they try?
qa.a: The teacher asked what felt bad and joined the groups on one rule; next time they could let Farhan help explain the shared rule to others.

qa.q: How might the two boys have felt when Farhan cried?
qa.a: They may have felt puzzled, since to them a new safe spot was just a game idea, not a break from the group.

grounding: Shows a child insisting on the same game rules as a group, since sameness feels safe to him.

passage: On the first day after the holidays at the village school, Charu, Deepu and Munni all had green water bottles from the Tuesday market. Kishore's was red. He hid it behind his back. At break, the three friends played 'tractor' with their green bottles as wheels, and Kishore stood and watched. That evening he cried until his mother promised to go to the market. 'Red is nice too,' she said. 'No! Everyone has green!' On Tuesday, holding his new green bottle, Kishore ran straight to join the tractor game.

qa.q: Where did the green water bottles come from?
qa.a: The Tuesday market.

qa.q: Why did Kishore hide his red bottle?
qa.a: He felt left out and embarrassed because his bottle was different from everyone else's.

qa.q: How could Kishore's mother or teacher help him feel included without buying the same things?
qa.a: Help him join the tractor game with his red bottle, showing that different colours can still play together.

qa.q: How might Charu see Kishore's new green bottle?
qa.a: Charu may simply be happy to have him join the game, perhaps without noticing how much the colour mattered to him.

grounding: A young child insists on the same bottle colour as his friends, because being different feels like being left out.
